beats.text: Picture a hospital ward at night. Every patient is connected to monitors.
An AI model reads their vital signs and lab results, and turns them into one number: the estimated chance of getting worse in the next twenty-four hours.
That number is an estimate. Not a diagnosis.
Now zoom out to a thousand patients, sorted by that estimated risk.
Nine hundred of them will be fine. A hundred will deteriorate. And the two groups overlap.
A threshold turns the score into an action. Set it at ten percent, and everyone to the right sends an alert to the nurse.
We catch most of the patients who will deteriorate, with about twenty false alarms.
Now, lower the threshold to five percent.
We catch almost everyone. But false alarms jump to around four hundred and fifty.
And here is the problem. With that many alerts, people stop reacting.
The one alert that really mattered gets swiped away with all the others. That is alert fatigue.
So there is no universal threshold. It is a trade-off between missed patients and false alarms.
And the right balance depends on the consequences, the staff, the model, and the patient.
